## Nivyx v2.4.0

A reliability and release-hardening release. Installing, updating and
uninstalling are now safe to fail on every platform, and an intermittent
Windows connection failure is fixed. How the DPI bypass works has not
changed.

### Windows
- Connections no longer fail now and then right after the service
  restarted. Windows reports a local port that is still closing from an
  earlier connection to the same server only late; such a connection is
  now retried from another port.
- `dpi-proxy.exe` opened from Explorer explains that it is the internal
  engine and changes nothing (before, it silently started a SOCKS5 proxy
  that protected nothing). From a terminal it behaves as before.
- `Install Nivyx.cmd` / `Uninstall Nivyx.cmd` return the real result:
  0 installed, 2 damaged package, 3 run from inside the ZIP, 4 failed and
  undone, 1223 administrator prompt declined, 6 Windows refused to start
  it elevated (e.g. by policy).
- A failed upgrade puts the previous version back and starts it.
- Service start failures say why (e.g. a blocked or damaged driver).
- `nivyx update` works when started from a PowerShell 7 window.
- The engine no longer reads any OpenSSL configuration file, and OpenSSL
  is built from the pinned official source (3.5.8).

### Linux
- A failed build or a missing dependency no longer stops a running
  Nivyx. A failed reinstall or migration restores the previous install,
  including installs from before v2.3.
- A plain uninstall keeps settings and learned state; `--purge` removes
  them.
- The update package runs on glibc 2.35 and newer (Debian 12, Ubuntu
  22.04 and later); the v2.3.0 package needed glibc 2.38.
- `nivyx repair` also recovers a service that systemd stopped restarting.
- Fedora and Arch (OpenSSL 4) install from source; the source build now
  works with OpenSSL 4. `nivyx update` explains this instead of failing.
- arm64 (e.g. Raspberry Pi 4/5) is tested in CI (install from source).

### macOS
- A plain uninstall keeps settings, learned state and logs; `--purge`
  removes them (before, everything was removed every time).
- A failed reinstall restores the previous installation; the launchers
  return the real exit code.
- The installer no longer strips the quarantine flag from the whole
  extracted folder.

### All platforms
- `nivyx update` verifies the download before unpacking it, backs up
  every file it replaces under a unique name, refuses packages with
  unexpected paths or links, restores the previous version if the
  health check fails and keeps its backup if even that fails.
- Only one install, update, repair or uninstall runs at a time.
- `nivyx status` reports "Active" only for a live engine.
- A data race between the DNS workers and the status writer was fixed.
- Releases now include `nivyx-release.manifest` (version and SHA-256 of
  every file), in addition to `SHA256SUMS`, the SPDX SBOM and signed
  GitHub build provenance.

### Release signatures: prepared, not enforced
The updater can check an Ed25519 signature on the release manifest
(refusing unsigned, tampered, substituted and downgraded releases), but
this is **not enabled**: no project signing key exists yet. Updates are
verified with SHA-256 against `SHA256SUMS`, as before. To check a
download yourself:
`gh attestation verify <file> --repo kadireren7/nivyx --source-ref refs/tags/v2.4.0`.

### Compatibility
Upgrading in place from v2.1.0, v2.2.x and v2.3.0 works, and the
`nivyx update` of v2.2.x and v2.3.0 installs this release on Linux,
macOS and Windows (the asset names and package layout they expect are
unchanged). Settings and learned state are kept.

### Testing and known limitations
- Tested automatically on GitHub-hosted machines: Ubuntu (x86_64 and
  arm64), Debian, openSUSE, Fedora, Arch, macOS 15 and 26 (Apple silicon
  and Intel) and Windows Server, including install, upgrade, update,
  rollback, repair and uninstall with real nftables, PF and WinDivert.
- **Not yet tested on physical consumer devices**: real Windows 10/11
  PCs with antivirus, real Macs (incl. macOS 11-14), Raspberry Pi
  hardware, sleep/resume and real DPI networks. Please report problems.
- On systemd 259 (e.g. Ubuntu 26.04), after `systemctl kill` HTTPS is
  refused for about 3 seconds until the service restarts; ordinary
  crashes and stops are not affected.
- Fedora and Arch: source install only (no prebuilt update package).
